title: The World's Slowest Experiments
description: A pitch drop a decade, a bell ringing since 1840 and a clock wound by Dunedin's weather

concepts.title: The Pitch Drop: A Liquid That Shatters
concepts.contentHtml:
In a glass cabinet at the University of Queensland in Brisbane, a funnel of black pitch has been dripping since 1930. Pitch, a tar derivative once used to waterproof boats, feels solid at room temperature and shatters under a hammer, yet it flows. Thomas Parnell, the university's first professor of physics, heated a sample in 1927, poured it into a glass funnel with a sealed stem, let it settle for three years and then cut the stem. Nine drops have fallen since.1

Nobody has ever watched one land. John Mainstone looked after the experiment for 52 years and never saw a drop fall. In 2000, when the eighth drop came down, the webcam set up to catch it failed at the critical moment. Mainstone died in August 2013, aged 78, with the ninth drop still on its way, though he did get to see video of a drop falling in Ireland.2 Trinity College Dublin had been running its own pitch drop since 1944. On July 11, 2013, a webcam there recorded a drop falling, the first time anyone had seen it happen.3

Why so slow? Viscosity measures how strongly a fluid resists flowing. A 1984 paper on the Queensland experiment put its pitch at about 250 billion times as viscous as water. In 2014 a UQ physicist estimated the forming tenth drop at about 30 billion times water, possibly because hot display lights had warmed the pitch by several degrees.4 Pitch thins sharply as it warms, so any single figure is a snapshot. Whether it counts as solid or liquid also depends on how long you watch: a hammer blow is far too quick for pitch to flow, so it cracks like glass, but over a decade it pours.

concepts.title: The Bell That Has Rung Since 1840
concepts.contentHtml:
In a display cabinet near the entrance of Oxford's Clarendon Laboratory, a small metal ball has been shuttling between two bells for nearly two centuries. A label in the handwriting of Robert Walker, Oxford's professor of physics from 1839 to 1865, reads "Set up in 1840", though a later note suggests it may have been built some 15 years earlier. The ringing is muffled, so visitors can see it but not hear it.1

The power comes from two dry piles, an early kind of battery. Exactly what is inside them is unknown, because opening them could end the experiment. A. J. Croft, a former Clarendon researcher, wrote in 1984 that the outer coating is sulfur, and that similar piles made by Giuseppe Zamboni stacked about 2,000 pairs of discs: tin foil glued to paper soaked in zinc sulfate, coated on the other side with manganese dioxide.2 Each pair is a feeble cell. Stacked in series, thousands of them add up to a large voltage, but they can push only a tiny current.

The ringing is electrostatics. The two piles are joined in series with a bell at each end, so the bells carry opposite charges. The ball, about 4 millimeters across, is drawn to one bell, touches it and takes on some of its charge. Now charged like that bell, it is pushed away and pulled toward the other, where it hands the charge over and picks up the opposite kind. Back and forth it goes, about twice a second, carrying a tiny packet of charge each trip. The bells have rung of the order of 10 billion times.3 Two taps a second since 1840 would come to more than 11 billion.

It is not perpetual motion. Guinness lists the bell as the world's most durable battery, and it will stop ringing when its clapper wears out or its stored chemical energy runs down.4 After nearly two centuries, neither has happened yet.

concepts.title: The Clock Wound by the Weather
concepts.contentHtml:
In the physics department of the University of Otago in Dunedin, New Zealand, stands a clock that, in principle, has not needed winding since Arthur Beverly made it in 1864. In practice it has stopped now and then: when its works needed cleaning, after a mechanical failure, when the department moved, and when the air temperature did not change enough.1

Beverly was a largely self-taught Scot, apprenticed at 13 to an optician and watchmaker in Aberdeen, who settled in Dunedin in 1858.2 His clock is wound by the weather. Inside is an airtight box of air. As the day warms, the air expands and pushes on a diaphragm; as it cools, the diaphragm sinks back. Changes in outside air pressure move it too. That motion lifts a weight, and the weight's slow fall drives the clock.3

So the clock is not a perpetual motion machine but a tiny heat engine, running on the gap between warm afternoons and cool nights. Otago physicist Craig Rodger says Beverly found that a daily temperature change of about 4 degrees Celsius was enough, and the clock's caretaker, Myles Thayer, says that in theory it could run forever.4 Warming sealed air by 4 degrees raises its pressure by only about 1.4 percent, but a clock needs very little energy, and Dunedin supplies a fresh swing every day. In 1984 the European Journal of Physics described the Beverly Clock, the Oxford bell and the Queensland pitch drop side by side: three of the longest-running experiments in the world, each in a university physics department.5

title: Discoveries That Weren't
description: N-rays in 300 papers, neutrinos faster than light and a Big Bang signal made of dust

concepts.title: N-Rays and the Missing Prism
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1903 René Blondlot, head of physics at the University of Nancy and a member of the French Academy of Sciences, announced a new kind of radiation. X-rays, found in 1895, had made new rays fashionable. Blondlot called his discovery N-rays, after his university. They were detected by eye, as a slight brightening of a faint spark or a dim phosphorescent screen. Soon other French researchers were finding them all over: Nancy's professor of medical physics, Augustin Charpentier, reported N-rays coming from living and dead bodies alike.1 At least 40 people said they had observed the effects, and about 100 scientists analyzed them in some 300 papers.2

Physicists elsewhere could see nothing. In September 1904 the American optics expert Robert Wood of Johns Hopkins University went to Nancy, as he later wrote in Nature, "in a doubting frame of mind".3 In a darkened room Blondlot showed him an aluminum prism that supposedly split a beam of N-rays into several beams, found by sliding a strip of phosphorescent paint along a curved support. While Blondlot took his readings, Wood secretly removed the prism. Blondlot got the same values as usual. In a later test Wood swapped a steel file, said to give off N-rays, for a wooden ruler of the same size, and the observer still saw the effect.4

Nobody needs to have lied. Judging whether a faint glow got slightly brighter is just where the eye sees what the mind expects. The chemist Irving Langmuir later made N-rays a classic case of pathological science: no dishonesty, just people "led astray by subjective effects, wishful thinking, or threshold interactions".5 Wood's trick is the standard remedy, now called blinding: whoever judges the result must not know which condition is which.

concepts.title: Faster Than Light? Check the Cable
concepts.contentHtml:
In September 2011 the OPERA experiment, under Italy's Gran Sasso mountain, reported something that should be impossible. Neutrinos sent from CERN, about 730 kilometers away, seemed to arrive about 60 billionths of a second sooner than light would have.1 Light makes that trip in about 2.4 thousandths of a second, so the lead was tiny, but in relativity nothing outruns light.

The team did not claim to have overturned Einstein. "This result comes as a complete surprise," said spokesperson Antonio Ereditato. The result rested on more than 15,000 neutrino events and pointed to a speed about 20 parts per million above light's, but months of checks had found no fault, so OPERA published it and asked for independent measurements.2

The culprit was mundane. A flight time is the difference between two clock readings 730 kilometers apart, kept in step by GPS. In February 2012 news reports citing people close to the experiment said a fiber-optic cable linking a GPS receiver to an electronic card in one of the lab computers had been found loose.3 An uncorrected delay in the timing chain shifts every arrival by the same amount; here it made the neutrinos look early.

Independent checks settled it. In March 2012 ICARUS, a Gran Sasso detector with its own timing, clocked seven neutrinos from CERN, all consistent with light speed. In June, four Gran Sasso experiments, OPERA included, agreed, and CERN attributed the original result to a faulty element of OPERA's fiber-optic timing system. A second suspect, a clock oscillator, worked in the opposite direction.4 OPERA's corrected figure was an arrival 6.5 billionths of a second early, with an uncertainty larger than that: no measurable difference from light.5

concepts.title: A Big Bang Signal Made of Dust
concepts.contentHtml:
On March 17, 2014, a team using the BICEP2 telescope at the South Pole announced the first direct evidence for cosmic inflation, the idea that in its first fleeting fraction of a second the universe expanded exponentially. The signal was stronger than many cosmologists expected. "This has been like looking for a needle in a haystack, but instead we found a crowbar," said co-leader Clem Pryke. The team had searched the cosmic microwave background, the faint afterglow of the Big Bang, for B-modes: a twisting, curl-like pattern in the direction of its polarization. Gravitational waves from inflation, squeezing space as they passed, should leave that kind of pattern.1

The team estimated that the dust models then available predicted far less contamination than the signal they saw.2 But dust grains in our own galaxy also give off polarized microwaves. BICEP2 had observed at a single frequency, which makes dust hard to tell apart from ancient light, whereas ESA's Planck satellite mapped the sky in nine frequency channels. In September 2014 Planck showed that polarized dust emission is significant across the entire sky and comparable to the BICEP2 signal even in the cleanest regions.3

So the teams pooled their data. The joint analysis, published in 2015, found strong evidence for dust and no statistically significant evidence for gravitational waves.4 Today the original Harvard press release opens with a correction: galactic dust contributes most of the BICEP2 signal, and only upper limits can be placed on gravitational waves.5 The search goes on, now at several frequencies at once. Dust and the Big Bang's afterglow change brightness differently from one frequency to the next, so measuring at several is how the two are told apart.

title: Measuring the World
description: Le Grand K's drifting copies, the meter's hidden error, and the leap second's last years

concepts.title: Le Grand K, the Kilogram That Drifted
concepts.contentHtml:
For more than a century, the kilogram was not a law of nature but a lump of metal. It was the mass of one golf-ball-sized cylinder of platinum and iridium, kept in a triple-locked vault on the outskirts of Paris and nicknamed Le Grand K.1

Forty near-identical copies were made at about the same time and, in 1889, handed out to member countries as national standards. Every few decades the copies came back to be compared with the original, and the results were awkward. By the 1946 check the copies were drifting away from Le Grand K on average, and by 1989–1991 the typical difference for the original set was about 25 micrograms, 25 millionths of a gram.2

So which was changing, the copies or the original? Nobody could say. Le Grand K was so precious that it was used to calibrate the world's standards only about once every 40 years. A metal object can wear, and gain or lose mass at any time, yet by definition Le Grand K weighed exactly one kilogram, with zero uncertainty. If it lost a few atoms, the kilogram itself shrank and every copy seemed to gain.3

The fix was to stop trusting objects. The kilogram is now defined by fixing a constant of nature, the Planck constant h, at exactly 6.626 070 15 × 10⁻³⁴ joule-seconds.4 Delegates representing 60 countries voted for the change at Versailles in November 2018, and it took effect on 20 May 2019. A kilogram can now be realized with a Kibble balance, named after its inventor Bryan Kibble: a current in a coil makes a magnetic force that holds up the mass, and quantum electrical measurements of current and voltage tie that force to h.5

concepts.title: The Meter and Méchain's Secret
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1792, in the middle of the French Revolution, two astronomers set out to measure the Earth. The new meter was to be one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator, scaled up from a survey of the Paris meridian from Dunkirk to Barcelona. Jean-Baptiste Delambre took the north and Pierre Méchain the harder south, across the Pyrenees.

Méchain's luck was terrible. He was arrested as a suspected counterrevolutionary, badly hurt by a hydraulic pump and stranded in Spain when war broke out. Stuck near Barcelona, he measured the latitude of Montjouy, just south of the city, and found it disagreed with his earlier figure for Barcelona by about three seconds of arc. Unable to find the cause and blaming himself, he kept the discrepancy a carefully guarded secret until his death in 1804.1

Only then did Delambre see the original notes. By then the meter had been built and declared law, so he kept the secret too, writing that he had "suppressed all those details which might diminish its confidence in such an important mission."2

The historian Ken Alder told the story in The Measure of All Things (2002). Méchain had doctored his records with an odd kind of honesty, making the altered readings look redundant so they would not be used at all. And his error is not why the meter is off. The finished meter came out about 0.2 millimeters short of its target, mainly because of wrong assumptions about the Earth's exact shape. Each later definition was calibrated to agree with the one before, so today's meter carries the same shortfall.3

Those definitions moved from metal to light: a platinum-iridium bar in 1889, wavelengths of light from krypton-86 in 1960 and, since 1983, the distance light travels in a set time.4 The speed of light is fixed at exactly 299,792,458 meters per second, so a meter is the distance light covers in 1/299,792,458 of a second.5

concepts.title: The Leap Second's Short, Buggy Life
concepts.contentHtml:
Some minutes have 61 seconds. On a leap-second night the world's official clocks read 23:59:59, then 23:59:60, then 00:00:00. The first leap second was added on June 30, 1972, and the point of all of them is to keep clock time within 0.9 seconds of time told by the turning Earth.1

The trouble is that we keep two kinds of time. Atomic clocks tick with near-perfect regularity, and the Earth does not. Over very long periods tides slow its spin, but it also speeds up and slows down from year to year, and lately it has at times spun slightly faster. To keep the two in step, 27 leap seconds were added between 1972 and the end of 2016.2

Computers hate them. Code for a 61-second minute almost never runs, so it is almost never tested. "Almost every time we have a leap second, we find something," Linux creator Linus Torvalds said in 2012, after that year's leap second tripped a Linux bug that hobbled Reddit, Gawker and Mozilla.3 The Amadeus Altea airline booking system went down for an hour, and staff at Qantas and Virgin Australia had to check passengers in by hand.4

The Earth's recent speed-up raised a scarier prospect: the first negative leap second, a second taken away, which no system has ever had to handle. In 2022 the world's metrology conference agreed to loosen the rule by 2035. In 2026 it went further, citing an expert estimate of a 30% chance of a negative leap second by 2035 and preparation costs on the scale of the millennium bug. From 20 May 2027 UTC will run continuously, and clock time may drift up to an hour from Earth time before anyone corrects it.5

title: Physics You Can Watch (but Can't Fully Explain)
description: The Oh-My-God particle, hot water that may freeze first, and why shaken big nuts rise

concepts.title: The Oh-My-God Particle
concepts.contentHtml:
On the night of October 15, 1991, the University of Utah's Fly's Eye detector at Dugway Proving Ground caught a cosmic ray with about 3.2 × 10²⁰ electron volts of energy. That is roughly the energy of a baseball traveling 55 miles per hour, carried by one particle smaller than an atom. It became known as the Oh-My-God particle.1

Fly's Eye never saw the particle itself. It recorded the shower of secondary particles the cosmic ray set off when it slammed into the air. The team reported 51 joules, far more than any cosmic ray seen before, and noted that the shower could not tell them what kind of particle it had been.2

That energy should be nearly impossible. Space is filled with microwave radiation left over from the Big Bang, and a particle this energetic loses energy as it plows through it, so it ought to come from fairly nearby. In 2021 the Telescope Array in Utah caught a second giant, named the Amaterasu particle after the Japanese sun goddess, at 2.4 × 10²⁰ eV. Traced back, it points toward the Local Void, an almost empty region bordering the Milky Way. "You trace its trajectory to its source and there's nothing high energy enough to have produced it," said John Matthews of the Telescope Array.3

Such particles carry about 10 million times the energy of those in the Large Hadron Collider, and nobody knows what accelerates them. A 2026 study suggests some may be nuclei heavier than iron, which lose energy more slowly and so could travel farther. Its authors are careful: "We are not saying that all ultrahigh-energy cosmic rays are ultraheavy nuclei."4

concepts.title: Mpemba's Ice Cream: Does Hot Water Freeze First?
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1963 Erasto Mpemba, a secondary school student in Tanzania, was making ice cream with his classmates. They were supposed to let their boiled-milk mixture cool before it went in the refrigerator, but space was scarce, so Mpemba put his in hot. It froze first. His teacher told him he must have been confused, and the class took to mocking his mistakes as "Mpemba's physics."

Mpemba kept experimenting. When Dr. Osborne, a professor from a nearby university, visited the school, Mpemba asked him why water at 100 °C froze faster than water at 35 °C. Osborne had a technician try it. The hot water froze first, and the technician added, "But we'll keep on repeating the experiment until we get the right result." The results held, and Mpemba and Osborne published them together in 1969.1

The idea is far older. Aristotle wrote that warmed water freezes more quickly, and Francis Bacon and René Descartes repeated the claim. But does it really happen? Explanations blame evaporation, dissolved gases, convection or supercooling. In 2016 Henry Burridge and Paul Linden reviewed the published data and cooled water under careful control. They found no evidence of a meaningful effect, and showed that a thermometer placed just 1 centimeter off could make an ordinary result look like one.2

The puzzle survives in a new form. In 2020 Avinash Kumar and John Bechhoefer showed a clean, repeatable Mpemba effect in a colloidal system immersed in water: with the right settings the hotter system cooled exponentially faster. Whether hot water beats cold in your freezer is still contested, but hot-first cooling is real physics.3

concepts.title: The Brazil Nut Effect
concepts.contentHtml:
Shake a can of mixed nuts long enough and the biggest end up on top. This Brazil nut effect also sorts stones and powders, and it causes real trouble: in drug manufacturing, separating powders can leave a blend uneven and throw off the dose in pills. It is not simple buoyancy. In one experiment both the heaviest and the lightest large balls rose faster than medium ones, and pumping the air out of the container changed the result.1

The old explanation was that small grains slip into the gaps that open beneath a big one with each shake, ratcheting it upward. In 1993 James Knight, Heinrich Jaeger and Sidney Nagel tracked a single large bead rising through a shaken column and found the main driver is granular convection. The grains circulate, rising up the middle and sliding down in a thin stream along the walls. The big bead rides the rising current to the top, and is too wide to fit into the narrow downward stream, so it stays stranded.2

The effect may even shape asteroids. Japan's Hayabusa spacecraft found that Itokawa, a small asteroid about 500 meters long, keeps its finest gravel in smooth patches while boulders cover its rough terrain. Researchers proposed that small meteoroid impacts shake the asteroid, fluidizing its loose rubble so the biggest pieces end up on the surface.3 Computer simulations support the idea: the Brazil nut effect still works in very weak gravity, only more slowly, and the shaking it needs is comparable to the tremors that small impacts would cause.4
